query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In equal‐ratio multimetal nanoparticles, the stability of the single-phase solid solution across the 473–1923 K operating range is governed by the interplay between thermally activated atomic diffusion and reactive environment‐induced surface segregation. Under catalytic (oxidative) conditions, selective oxidation of more reactive elements (e.g., Cr, Al) rapidly forms a thin, protective oxide layer that limits further diffusion and phase separation, thereby maintaining structural and chemical integrity; in contrast, under thermoelectric (inert) conditions, the absence of such an oxide barrier permits enhanced atomic mobility leading to elemental segregation and microstructural destabilization.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles comprising five or more metals in near-equiatomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles from 473 to 1923 K under two controlled atmospheres: an oxidative (catalytic) environment versus an inert (thermoelectric) environment.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted using in situ high-resolution TEM with EDS mapping and synchrotron XRD; nanoparticles must contain reactive elements (e.g., Cr or Al) capable of forming protective oxides; temperature ramps and hold times should be sufficient to activate atomic diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or absence) of a reactive-element-derived surface oxide layer that acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, atomic diffusion is thermally activated. In an oxidative environment, reactive elements are preferentially oxidized at the nanoparticle surface, generating a passivating oxide layer that hampers further atom migration and inhibits phase separation, whereas in an inert atmosphere, lacking such passivation, unmitigated diffusion leads to surface segregation and eventual structural decomposition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under catalytic (oxidative) conditions, nanoparticles will exhibit a thin, self-limiting oxide layer with minimal bulk chemical segregation, preserving the solid solution phase. Under inert conditions, more pronounced atomic rearrangements and phase separation (segregation) will be observed, leading to detectable changes in the lattice structure compared to the initial state.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized nanoparticles with homogeneous, equimolar solid solution structure at room temperature prior to thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds for nanoparticles whose composition includes sufficient reactive elements to form protective oxides. If nanoparticles lack these elements, or if grain sizes are extremely small (altering diffusion dynamics), the mechanism and outcomes may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative rates of oxide formation versus atomic diffusion and the exact temperature thresholds for initiating segregation are not precisely known and may vary with nanoparticle size and specific elemental composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical batches of equimolar high-entropy nanoparticles and subject them to identical heating profiles (473–1923 K) under both an oxidative and an inert atmosphere. Use in situ high-resolution TEM with EDS mapping as well as synchrotron XRD to monitor phase evolution, elemental segregation, and surface oxide formation in real time.
measurements: Surface composition and thickness of any oxide layers (via TEM-EDS mapping)
Changes in lattice parameters and phase identification (via synchrotron XRD)
Atomic diffusion rates and evidence of elemental segregation (via in situ TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles heated in the oxidative environment do not exhibit a protective oxide layer or show similar degrees of atomic segregation and phase decomposition as those in the inert environment, the hypothesis that selective oxidation governs stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
